Could you provide a single document that covers: the test harness you use (traffic synthesis, hardware mix), representative run artifacts (quantile series, heatmaps), and a short narrative on mitigation controls (fallbacks, cache priming, graceful degradation)? Subject: Re: RFP: evidence for performance oscillation + scaling behaviour

Alex — thanks for the clear ask. Attached is a compact evidence pack that maps our test harness, raw artifacts and an executive narrative. Key highlights up front: 

- Test harness: 3-layer generator (client, ingress-proxy, backend worker) that replays traffic_matrix.json across model families (decoder-only 7B, 13B; decoder-encoder 6B) and quantization profiles. Each run used a deterministic seed and included sustained 60-minute windows with 5- and 30-minute microburst phases. Hardware: mix of A800 and RTX 6000 gen2 nodes to reflect heterogenous fleets.

- Oscillation detection: We compute rolling quantiles (50/90/99) on a 1s sampling basis and a 60s EWMA to find oscillatory modes. In the attached latency_heatmaps.csv you will see two recurring signatures: (A) batching amplification when concurrent request mix shifts from short (<=64 tokens) to long (>512 tokens) leading to kernel-recompilation-like spikes, and (B) KV-cache eviction cascades after prefix churn in high fanout multi-user tests. Both signatures are transient and bounded by our mitigation policies.

- Scaling behavior and control plane actions: Our autoscaler uses a three-tier policy: immediate burst replicas (15–30s spin-up using warm image pool), steady-scale (2–5m smoothing window) and background reclaim (10–30m). We backstop with model-variant fallbacks (lower-seq-length quantized variant) and region-level routing to avoid head-of-line blocking. Empirical evidence in redwood_perf_runbook.pdf illustrates a 2.3x throughput increase with linearized latency growth for steady ramps up to 10k QPS for the tested workload profile.

- Correlations to system-level signals: We capture kernel scheduling stall traces, CUDA kernel selection logs and driver-level retry counts. Where we observed transient 99.9th spikes, they correlated with short-lived kernel selection path changes when sequence length distribution shifted abruptly; we reduce this by pre-warming kernel caches for the predicted distribution. See runbook section 4.2 and the sample trace IDs in the Drive link.

I included three artifacts: redwood_perf_runbook.pdf (narrative + plots), latency_heatmaps.csv (quantiles over time with tags), traffic_matrix.json (input mix). If you want raw collector traces (eBPF slices/CUDA logs) we can provide redacted snippets under NDA.

Next steps: would you like a short live walk-through of the artifacts with our SRE engineer? We can run a tailored surge test against a Cloudfolio-like request distribution.

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Director, Product - Inference
Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood_perf_runbook.pdf (application/pdf), latency_heatmaps.csv (text/csv), traffic_matrix.json (application/json)

Alex — a couple small clarifications to make sure the artifacts map to your acceptance criteria: 

1) Which quantiles do your SRE reviewers prioritize for acceptance? We report 50/90/95/99/99.9 by default, but if you need 99.99 we can extend the collector.
2) Do you need multi-tenant (synthetic tenants with noisy neighbors) vs single-tenant soak runs separated? Our multi-tenant evidence shows higher KV-cache churn — we included one multi-tenant trace but can split it out.
3) Are there particular hardware families or driver versions you must see proof for (e.g., A100 vs A800)? We tested multiple generations — the runbook lists versions.

If you prefer, we can schedule a 45-minute session where we replay a 15-minute microburst live against a Cloudfolio-shaped workload and stream the quantile charts. That often answers the acceptance questions faster than static docs.

Soojin Lee
Senior SRE, Inference
Redwood Inference
